Everyday Sparks 2.0: Deepening Routine Writing

🖼️ Framing Our Work

Building on the work you began in Cultivating Literacy Routines in the fall, this module focuses on sustaining and deepening the writing practices you’ve established in your classroom. Many teachers find it easy to begin routine writing in the fall but more challenging to sustain it throughout the year. Students may tire of familiar activities, other demands can shift a teacher’s focus, and it’s not always clear how to deepen the learning as routines become more established. This module invites you to explore strategies for keeping routine writing fresh, purposeful, and responsive to your students as the year progresses.


📝What to Expect

In this module, you will:

✅Revisit the principles of Everyday Sparks and explore how to sustain daily and weekly writing routines throughout the year

✅ Learn three strategies for keeping writing fresh and purposeful—Finding Topics with a Daily Schedule, Interpreting Visual Texts to Deepen Thinking, and Take a Line for a Walk

✅ Reflect on how these strategies can help students continue to grow as writers and thinkers

✅ Earn the Everyday Sparks 2.0: Deepening Routine Writing discussion badge for contributing to the discussion and sharing your reflections

✅ Earn the Everyday Sparks microcredential by reflecting with your facilitator on how you will adapt these strategies for your own students, including sharing a draft or example from your classroom.

🧭 Explore and Learn

Below is an excerpt from Atomic Habits by James Clear. Though his book is not specifically about teaching, it can provide insight into how humans improve their skills.


The Danger of Aiming for Perfection On the first day of class, Jerry Uelsmann, a professor at the University of Florida, divided his film photography students into two groups. Everyone on the left side of the classroom, he explained, would be in the “quantity” group. They would be graded solely on the amount of work they produced. On the final day of class, he would tally the number of photos submitted by each student. One hundred photos would rate an A, ninety photos a B, eighty photos a C, and so on. Meanwhile, everyone on the right side of the room would be in the “quality” group. They would be graded only on the excellence of their work. They would only need to produce one photo during the semester, but to get an A, it had to be a nearly perfect image. At the end of the term, he was surprised to find that all the best photos were produced by the quantity group. During the semester, these students were busy taking photos, experimenting with composition and lighting, testing out various methods in the darkroom, and learning from their mistakes. In the process of creating hundreds of photos, they honed their skills. Meanwhile, the quality group sat around speculating about perfection. In the end, they had little to show for their efforts other than unverified theories and one mediocre photo. It is easy to get bogged down trying to find the optimal plan for change: the fastest way to lose weight, the best program to build muscle, the perfect idea for a side hustle. We are so focused on figuring out the best approach that we never get around to taking action. As Voltaire once wrote, “The best is the enemy of the good.”

The excerpt from Atomic Habits reminds us that growth comes from consistent practice, not from waiting for the perfect conditions. The same is true for writing. Our students don’t become stronger writers because of one polished piece—they grow through the daily and weekly habits that invite them to practice, experiment, and learn from their attempts.

Sustaining these routines through the year means finding ways to keep them meaningful, varied, and connected to students’ lives and classroom learning. Below are three adaptable strategies that can help you keep writing routines fresh while deepening students’ thinking.

Daily Schedule

In the fall, you explored Quicklists as a strategy for helping students generate writing ideas. Finding ideas is not a one-time skill; it’s something students (and teachers) continue to practice as they grow as writers. This strategy returns to that same goal—supporting writers in discovering topics worth writing about—but with a new variation.

This activity helps writers notice that meaningful writing topics are often hiding in plain sight. It’s a way to sustain engagement by showing students that their daily experiences can inspire authentic questions and arguments worth writing about.

The idea is to help students find writing topics in their daily schedules. Students can use a clock organizer or create one in their writing notebooks, then chart out how they spend 12 hours in a typical day. They can also simply list their schedule. After recording their schedule, they look back over it to identify possible topics, issues, or questions worth exploring. Notice the example below. From this schedule, a teacher generated a topic list in the form of questions:

  • Is breakfast really the most important meal of the day?

  • Best approaches to dog training?

  • Would a block schedule help mitigate learning loss?

  • What are the mental health benefits of taking breaks and going outside?

  • Are there benefits to doing nothing? Is it okay to do nothing?

Schedule by Greg Raney, South Coast Writing Project at UC Santa Barbara

Interpreting Visual Texts to Deepen Thinking

In her book This Is Disciplinary Literacy: Reading, Writing, Thinking, and Doing... Content Area by Content Area, ReLeah Cossett Lent reminds us that,

In case anyone hasn't noticed, we are teaching a generation that loves visuals. Just because students are inundated with visuals doesn't mean they know how to read them. . . So, providing more visuals to students may not be enough; we must help students learn to read visuals as they would any other text and understand how they are used to construct (or skew) meaning in each discipline...

Visual literacy is important because we know that non-linguistic representations of a concept, especially when paired with print, can increase students' ability to learn (Marzano, Pickering, & Pollock, 2001). Many students who have difficulty with print-centric text can find meaning from illustrations, graphs, diagrams, and other visuals, but they often need guidance in deciphering such text accurately. Conversely, students who are good readers may have difficulty with visual text. Reading visually is a skill that should be taught in every discipline.



Building on the ideas from the fall Reading to Write: They Say / I Say module, this reminder invites us to think about how visual texts can support increasingly complex reading and writing work. Cognitive research shows that learning often proceeds from the concrete to the abstract, and from the visual to the nonvisual. When we bring this understanding into our literacy routines, visuals become a powerful bridge to higher-level thinking.

As we sustain writing routines throughout the year, visual texts can offer a way to raise the cognitive demand while maintaining accessibility. To that end, you might:

  • Provide more complex visuals (such as infographics, charts, or graphs) and guide students in analyzing them.

  • Use simple visuals (such as photographs or political cartoons) to help students practice more complex skills, like analyzing tone, evaluating perspective, or inferring bias.

Routine writing connected to visuals can move beyond observation to interpretation and argument. To support these more complex and targeted kinds of visual interpretations, Lent provides a list of "Questions for Interpreting Visual Text," (page 43) which are included in the slideshow below as possibilities for engaging your students in analyzing a visual text. The slideshow also includes a number of visuals you might want to try out with your students. You are encouraged to make a copy of the slideshow and choose the questions and visual(s) that are the best fit for your students and instructional goals.


If you are interested in finding other visual texts for a specific topic or writing task, check out these resources:

Take a Line for a Walk

You can get the most benefits from routine writing when it connects to the work already happening in your classroom. One simple way to do this is through a quick activity called Take a Line for a Walk.

For this strategy, choose a text or excerpt you are already planning to have your students read. Have them open their Writer’s Notebooks, select a line that stands out to them, and copy it onto a fresh page. Then, invite them to “take that line for a walk” by writing in response—following wherever their thoughts lead. Students might agree or disagree with the line, connect it to something in their own lives, explore its implications, or simply reflect on why it caught their attention.

After writing, you might invite students to share what they discovered—first with a partner or small group, and then perhaps as a whole class. Over time, this simple practice helps students strengthen the habit of using writing to make meaning from texts and see connections between what they read, what they think, and what they write.

💬 Try and Share

For the Everyday Sparks 2.0 discussion, you’ll have two options for trying out one of the strategies from this module. Choose the one that feels most useful or inspiring to you right now.

Option 1: Interpreting Visual Texts Use one of the resources provided above, or another resource you know of, to find a complex visual text—an infographic, chart, photo, or other image—related to your content area that you might use with students. In your post, share the visual text and a few notes about how and why you would use it. You might also include one or two interpretation questions you would ask to guide student thinking.

Option 2: Take a Line for a Walk Choose a line from the Atomic Habits or This Is Disciplinary Literacy excerpts in this module and “take it for a walk.” Copy the line into your Writer’s Notebook (or document), then write in response, following your thoughts wherever they lead. In your post, share the line you chose and some or all of your writing, along with a brief reflection about what the experience was like for you.

After posting, be sure to read and respond to at least two other teachers’ posts. Notice what ideas or possibilities stand out to you as you read each other’s work!

Breanna Smith
1:54 pm

I chose option 2: Take a Line for a walk. The line I chose is this, "They would be graded only on the excellence of their work." I chose this because while the quality of a student's final product is important, grading should not be based only on the excellence of the work. This approach overlooks student growth, effort, use of feedback, and the learning process itself. Many students make significant progress even if their final product is not "excellent," and assessment should reflect mastery over time, engagement with the task, and alignment to learning goals... not just a polished outcome. We simply want our students to learn and grow as learners. Expecting them to produce excellent work every time and solely setting the grading based on that...is setting them up for failure. This process wasn't that bad for me to do. It helped that I picked a line that I felt I could back up and support my viewpoints on it pretty well.

I used a photosynthesis infographic from National Geographic Education to support students in interpreting complex visual texts. I chose option 2: Take a Line for a walk. The line I chose is this, "They would be graded only on the excellence of their work." I chose this because while the quality of a student's final product is important, grading should not be based only on the excellence of the work. This approach overlooks student growth, effort, use of feedback, and the learning process itself. Many students make significant progress even if their final product is not "excellent," and assessment should reflect mastery over time, engagement with the task, and alignment to learning goals... not just a polished outcome. We simply want our students to learn and grow as learners. Expecting them to produce excellent work every time and solely setting the grading based on that...is setting them up for failure. What do you notice and what do you wonder?

What do you think the y axis label is and why? Then reveal it.

What do you think the x axis label is and why? Then reveal it.

What do you think it means for a food to be on the trend line, above the trend line or on the trend line?

I like this writing exercise for myself and my students.  It is a low stakes writing practice that lets us use deep thinking skills and self reflection.  I think the students will enjoy it because they can choose any line in a text, not one that is given by the teacher, and pick one that resonates with them.  That will make the writing easier for them because they have their own thoughts on why they picked that particular line, which in turn makes it more meaningful for them.

My administrator introduced me to a strategy called Save the Last Word for Me. It is very similar to this writing exercise. All the students read a shared text and then on an index card they each write one powerful quote from the text. On the back of the index card they write an explanation for why they picked that quote. The students will then meet in a small group and take turns sharing only the quote they picked with the group. The group discussesWhat stands out?

  • Why might this be important?

  • What does it reveal about the text?

I chose Option 1: Interpreting Visual Texts as a strategy to try and prepare to use in my own classroom. We are currently discussing DNA replication, protein synthesis, and building up to discussing meiosis. This time of year is really fun for students because we get to discuss complex diseases and genetic abnormalities. I chose a cartoon from the amoeba sisters line of cartoons that discusses the role of mRNA in getting the genetic code out of the nucleus. The purpose of getting the genetic code out of the nucleus is to make proteins. I would show my students this cartoon and give them the following discussion questions: What does this cartoon tell you about the location of transcription and translation in the cell? Why can only the mRNA strand leave the nucleus? What is the primary goal of using mRNA to get the genetic code out of the nucleus? I would do this by printing (or posting on a Google doc) the visual onto a piece of paper along with the questions, and leave lines at the bottom for students to write their answers. Then, I would have students discuss their answers in pairs, then as a whole group. You could also provide multiple cartoons (or visual texts) for students to interpret in a gallery walk setting, and have them post their thoughts around the images as well. There are definitely many ways to adapt this activity! I think this could be really fun!

I chose the second option - Take a line for a walk. I actually wrote 3 lines from Atomic Habits that all related to each other. 1. "Habits are the compound of interest of self-improvement." 2. "If you can get 1 percent better each day for one year, you'll end up thirty-seven times better by the time you're done." 3. "You should be far more concerned with your current trajectory than with your current results." If we focus on getting a little better each day and create small habits over a span of time, we will be able to make changes without being overwhelmed. Many times, when we try to make changes or create new habits, we go "all in" and usually burn out quickly, so focusing on the 1 percent each day and how that compounds over time is much more motivating. Another problem with habits, goals, and making changes is that we focus so much on where are currently. Most of the time, it takes consistent actions over time before we notice a change. This can be very discouraging and leads to many people quitting whatever goal they are working towards. If we focus more on the trajectory and where we are headed, we would be more motivated to keep up with the habits necessary to accomplish the goal.

Breanna Smith

I chose option 2: Take a Line for a walk. The line I chose is this, "They would be graded only on the excellence of their work." I chose this because while the quality of a student's final product is important, grading should not be based only on the excellence of the work. This approach overlooks student growth, effort, use of feedback, and the learning process itself. Many students make significant progress even if their final product is not "excellent," and assessment should reflect mastery over time, engagement with the task, and alignment to learning goals... not just a polished outcome. We simply want our students to learn and grow as learners. Expecting them to produce excellent work every time and solely setting the grading based on that...is setting them up for failure. This process wasn't that bad for me to do. It helped that I picked a line that I felt I could back up and support my viewpoints on it pretty well.

I chose this option as well. I thought of choosing the quote you chose too! I really liked that one - it goes well with the one I ended up choosing - "You should be far more concerned with your current trajectory than with your current results." I feel like this matters because one reason we give up before we reach our goals is because we want that instant gratification. When we see where we are right now, and it seems so far away, or isn't "excellent," it can feel too overwhelming. If we look at our trajectory, on the otherhand, we can see that the progress is compounding and that is much more motivating.

Many people complain about the age of our law makers in Washington, D.C., so to introduce the Legislative Branch I had students examine a chart that showed the age groups of the House of Representatives and the Senate. I began with a breif, whole class discussion about what the graph showed. I wanted to make sure students understood they were looking the distribution of ages grouped by decades (20-29, 30-39, etc.). Then, I asked them to respond to the prompt: Why does it matter who represents us?

I was a little disappointed that many students seemed to ignore the topic of the chart in their response. For example, "It matters who represents us because you want someone who's wise and knows cause and effect, but you also want someone who people will listen to and respect while still respecting others." Fortunately, some students did make the connection. However, their thinking surprised me. Several students had a response similar to this: "I think it does matter who represents us because if its an older person they have more experience to life so they might have the best options and opportunities to represent us."

In hindsight, I would make my question more specific. I might ask, How does age of our representatives impact the way people represent us?

I chose a line from This is Disciplinary Literacy: "So providing more visuals to students may not be enough; we must help students learn to read visuals as they would any other text and understand how they are used to construct (or show) meaning in each discipline." I feel like today's consumption of information is largely visual, and students (and many adults) are often quick to take things at face value without spending time reflecting on what is actually be said or not said in visual text. I stole a strategy from Kelly Gallagher several years ago that uses just that: What is being said? What is not being said? Further, I spend time teaching students, usually upper level high schoolers, how to pay attention to graphics and the population used in such graphics. For example, when they see a graph or other data set sharing polling information or a survey that "50% of Americans__________", I tell them to go to that original survey and look at the population used in it; oftentimes, that "50%" was a total of 1500 participants--which is far from a legit "50%" of our population! It's pretty eye-opening for students, especially those on the brink of becoming voting citizens, when they realize how easily data can be misrepresented. Regardless of political or other beliefs, understanding how visual information is presented and represented is crucial to being a truly literate, informed individual.

In an 8th-grade heredity unit, this activity on Polydactyly would be used as an engaging way to connect vocabulary, visual analysis, and genetic reasoning. I would begin by showing students the image of the hand and the word “polydactyly,” asking them to break the term into parts (“poly” meaning many and “dactyl” meaning fingers or toes) so they can infer that the condition involves having extra digits. This approach helps students build confidence in decoding scientific terms while making the concept more memorable. Next, I would introduce the pedigree chart and guide students in interpreting its symbols and patterns, helping them understand how traits are tracked across generations. Rather than directly telling them whether the trait is dominant or recessive, I would use prompting questions to guide their thinking, such as asking them to look for patterns like whether the trait appears in every generation or skips generations. These questions encourage students to rely on evidence from the pedigree, leading them to conclude that polydactyly is a dominant trait because it consistently appears in each generation and affected parents pass it to their children. Overall, the prompting questions are essential because they scaffold student thinking, promote critical analysis, and reinforce the practice of using evidence to support scientific conclusions rather than simply memorizing facts.

As a middle school science teacher, I chose to use a visual diagram of the rock cycle as my complex visual text. This type of diagram typically shows how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks are connected through processes like weathering, erosion, heat, pressure, melting, and cooling.

I would use this visual in my classroom during our Earth science unit when introducing how rocks change over time. The rock cycle is a great example of a system that is not linear, and students often struggle with the idea that rocks can move between different types through multiple pathways. This visual helps students see the cyclical nature of Earth’s processes and reinforces key vocabulary in a meaningful context.

I would first have students observe the diagram independently and write down what they notice. Then, we would discuss it as a class, focusing on how different processes connect the rock types. This supports both science understanding and literacy skills by encouraging students to interpret and explain visual information.

To guide student thinking, I would ask questions such as:

  • “What processes cause a rock to change from one type to another?”

  • “Can a rock follow more than one pathway in this diagram? Explain your reasoning using evidence from the visual.”

Using a visual text like this allows students to practice interpreting scientific diagrams while also building deeper conceptual understanding. It also supports diverse learners by providing a non-text-based entry point into complex content.

I chose a line from This is Disciplinary Literacy: "So providing more visuals to students may not be enough; we must help students learn to read visuals as they would any other text and understand how they are used to construct (or show) meaning in each discipline." I feel like today's consumption of information is largely visual, and students (and many adults) are often quick to take things at face value without spending time reflecting on what is actually be said or not said in visual text. I stole a strategy from Kelly Gallagher several years ago that uses just that: What is being said? What is not being said? Further, I spend time teaching students, usually upper level high schoolers, how to pay attention to graphics and the population used in such graphics. For example, when they see a graph or other data set sharing polling information or a survey that "50% of Americans__________", I tell them to go to that original survey and look at the population used in it; oftentimes, that "50%" was a total of 1500 participants--which is far from a legit "50%" of our population! It's pretty eye-opening for students, especially those on the brink of becoming voting citizens, when they realize how easily data can be misrepresented. Regardless of political or other beliefs, understanding how visual information is presented and represented is crucial to being a truly literate, informed individual.

I chose option 1, however I am interested in using option 2 in my core classes that I teach. It is interesting when you dig deeper what you find out and how media will skew information to suit their platform or agenda.

Interpreting Visual Text

I used this image (The First Thanksgiving 1621) to practice three skills important to the work of historians - sourcing, contextualization, and corroboration.

Sourcing: Who created this source? When was this source created? Why do you think this source was created?

Contextualization: What historical event is depicted in this image? What was happening in Plymouth in 1621? What was happening in 1932 in America when this image was created?

Corroboration: Is this source historically accurate? What do other sources say about the historical event? Can we use this source as evidence to support other historical accounts?

Breanna Smith

I chose option 2: Take a Line for a walk. The line I chose is this, "They would be graded only on the excellence of their work." I chose this because while the quality of a student's final product is important, grading should not be based only on the excellence of the work. This approach overlooks student growth, effort, use of feedback, and the learning process itself. Many students make significant progress even if their final product is not "excellent," and assessment should reflect mastery over time, engagement with the task, and alignment to learning goals... not just a polished outcome. We simply want our students to learn and grow as learners. Expecting them to produce excellent work every time and solely setting the grading based on that...is setting them up for failure. This process wasn't that bad for me to do. It helped that I picked a line that I felt I could back up and support my viewpoints on it pretty well.

Breanna, I love your way of thinking on grading their work. I do feel this was a great option for students to choose instead of being given something they might not connect with.

As a middle school science teacher, I chose to use a visual diagram of the rock cycle as my complex visual text. This type of diagram typically shows how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks are connected through processes like weathering, erosion, heat, pressure, melting, and cooling.

I would use this visual in my classroom during our Earth science unit when introducing how rocks change over time. The rock cycle is a great example of a system that is not linear, and students often struggle with the idea that rocks can move between different types through multiple pathways. This visual helps students see the cyclical nature of Earth’s processes and reinforces key vocabulary in a meaningful context.

I would first have students observe the diagram independently and write down what they notice. Then, we would discuss it as a class, focusing on how different processes connect the rock types. This supports both science understanding and literacy skills by encouraging students to interpret and explain visual information.

To guide student thinking, I would ask questions such as:

  • “What processes cause a rock to change from one type to another?”

  • “Can a rock follow more than one pathway in this diagram? Explain your reasoning using evidence from the visual.”

Using a visual text like this allows students to practice interpreting scientific diagrams while also building deeper conceptual understanding. It also supports diverse learners by providing a non-text-based entry point into complex content.

As someone who believes science is magic and rocks are rocks I would truly appreciate a visual. Being able to give the words a deeper connection beyond the text and see a real-world application would be huge to many of our struggling readers!

Many people complain about the age of our law makers in Washington, D.C., so to introduce the Legislative Branch I had students examine a chart that showed the age groups of the House of Representatives and the Senate. I began with a breif, whole class discussion about what the graph showed. I wanted to make sure students understood they were looking the distribution of ages grouped by decades (20-29, 30-39, etc.). Then, I asked them to respond to the prompt: Why does it matter who represents us?

I was a little disappointed that many students seemed to ignore the topic of the chart in their response. For example, "It matters who represents us because you want someone who's wise and knows cause and effect, but you also want someone who people will listen to and respect while still respecting others." Fortunately, some students did make the connection. However, their thinking surprised me. Several students had a response similar to this: "I think it does matter who represents us because if its an older person they have more experience to life so they might have the best options and opportunities to represent us."

In hindsight, I would make my question more specific. I might ask, How does age of our representatives impact the way people represent us?

I think it would be interesting to give them a different age chart on something that they feel directly impacts them and see how they feel. Maybe politics is to far removed from their daily life. What if you changed the title to age of people that decide who can post Tik Tok videos or something silly like that. They may have very strong opinions then...
